newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr stuck mid-range, lost for direction.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr stuck mid-range, lost for direction.

text.p: The Australian dollar eked out a meagre trading range at the midsession with today's RBA board meeting rendered largely irrelevant by the latest rate cut.
The failure of the dollar to follow through on last week's short covering rally and the resulting lapse into its old trading band has left the market lost for direction.
Technicals were mostly bearish following the cut below US$0.7440 and argued for an extension of the five month-old downtrend to at least US$0.7250 and possibly US$0.7070.
But dealers remembered how impressive bids had been around US$0.7330 and were not keen to chase the currency lower.

By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had settled at US$0.7400/05 having started at US$0.7405/10 from US$0.7390/95 late Monday. That was up on its US$0.7365 low but a long way from last week's US$0.7505 high.
On the crosses it pulled back on the mark after touching fresh five year highs around 1.3827 overnight, to stand at 1.3755/71 marks from 1.3778/93 late here Monday.

It was steady on the yen at 87.53/63 from 87.47/57 and was at 58.1 in trade weighted terms from a previous 58.0. But it lost ground to the Kiwi after New Zealand jobs data proved less weak than expected and monetary conditions tightened somewhat.
The Kiwi firmed to US$0.6441/48 from US$0.6425/30 while the A$ eased to NZ$1.1476/97 from NZ$1.1505/25.
Labour data are much on the mind of the local market as dealers suspect a weak employment result for July could start the money market looking yet another easing in policy.
The data, due Thursday, are expected to show an employment gain of around 25,000 but also a rise in the unemployment rate to 8.6 percent from 8.5 percent.
Such a job increase would be twice June's 11,900 gain but even together would not compensate for May's 40,300 drop, so anything less could start the rate whispers once again.
Most analysts reckoned there was enough stimulus in the pipeline -- the 0.5 point cut in official rates to 5.0 percent was the fifth in a year -- to promote a pickup in growth.

But signs of strength had mainly been confined to leading indicators so far and the inflation outlook was so favourable the central bank might feel there was little risk in taking further insurance on a recovery.
The bank's board holds its monthly meeting today but is less important now that the RBA has expressely severed the link between meetings and the timing of changes in policy.
